Image-based fruit inventories count fruit from photographs, but a camera moving along a row or around a tree sees most fruit several times, so a sum of detections overstates the true number.
This review examines how the literature decides which observations belong to the same fruit and how class labels such as maturity are attached to each unique fruit.
A systematic search of Scopus identified 971 relevant studies published between 2012 and 2026.

The 187 studies that combine several observations of the same fruit were classified into six association mechanisms: no association, statistical correction, appearance matching, temporal tracking, geometric or 3D association, and learned association.
Temporal tracking dominates recent work, and geometric association provides the most direct calibration-free counts when camera pose and depth are reliable.
On fruit that look alike, appearance features did not improve tracking over motion alone.
Few studies report identity errors or counts per class, and comparisons of mechanisms on the same data are rare.
In oil palm, published work concentrates on ripeness classification and bunch detection in single images; cross-view association of bunches on a palm has not been evaluated.
The review relates each mechanism to the acquisition conditions it requires and proposes the measurements needed to evaluate duplicate-aware, class-wise inventories.

Each included study was assigned to one of seven groups: multi-observation studies, which combine several observations of the same fruit (video, several views, or repeated scans); single-view counting and yield studies; oil-palm fresh-fruit-bunch (FFB) imaging studies, including mill grading and loose fruit; studies that count fruit by class in single images; depth, 3D, and non-RGB sensing studies; earlier reviews; and methods papers from outside agriculture.

The second is the 19 multi-observation studies that report counts per class.
None of the 19 abstracts describes how a label is chosen when frames disagree, and none reports a class confusion matrix computed on unique fruit.
The 129 depth and 3D sensing studies use RGB-D cameras (74), stereo (19), LiDAR (13), or other non-RGB signals.
Their main use is not association but detection, localization, and sizing of individual fruit, most often apples (46).

Fig. (ref) shows that the 170 oil-palm studies concentrate on ripeness: 76 classify the ripeness of images of single bunches, 37 detect bunches in a scene, 21 study non-RGB sensing of ripeness, 12 address quality, defects, mass, or pose, 10 detect loose fruit, 9 count bunches, and 4 are dataset papers.
The setting is on the palm in 40 studies, at a mill, conveyor, or laboratory in 25, on the ground in 13, and from a UAV in 4; 88 abstracts do not state it.
Class labels are attached to instances in 132 studies.
Only 11 use more than one view of the same bunch or tree.
G1: Identity is rarely measured. Only 13% of the multi-observation studies report an identity metric in the abstract.
G2: Mechanisms are rarely compared on the same data. Table (ref) contains 13 such comparisons, most within M3.

Abstracts were not available from the database export used and were retrieved from other bibliographic services; 254 records without an abstract were decided from titles, sources, and machine-generated summaries.
Open-access full text was available for about a third of the included studies (331 of 971), so most coding relied on abstracts.
The 187 multi-observation studies in this map use six mechanisms to decide which observations belong to the same fruit.
